source.title: Soil Classification Dataset (seven original image classes)

Alluvial Soil.description: A broad label for soil material deposited by flowing water. Texture and fertility vary by site.
characteristics: May range from coarse sand to fine silt or clay.
An image cannot establish depth, drainage, fertility, or flood risk.
advantages: Some deep, well-managed alluvial soils support a wide range of crops.
limitations: Flooding, erosion, coarse texture, or poor drainage may occur depending on the site.
improvements: Use a representative soil test before changing nutrients or pH.
Maintain ground cover and assess field drainage and flood exposure.

crop_guidance.note: NCERT lists these as crops suited to alluvial soils in general. They are examples, not a location-specific recommendation; confirm season, water, and local conditions.
crop_guidance.source_title: NCERT, Contemporary India-II, Chapter 1: Resources and Development — Alluvial Soils

Arid Soil.description: A dataset label associated with arid-region soils; it does not by itself identify salinity or water-holding capacity.
characteristics: Water availability and organic matter can be limiting in dry settings.
Salt accumulation is possible in some irrigated areas but must be measured.
advantages: Crop choices can be adapted to locally verified rainfall and irrigation availability.
limitations: Water stress and salt risk vary substantially between fields.
improvements: Check soil electrical conductivity and irrigation-water quality before treatment.
Use locally appropriate mulch, residue cover, and erosion control.

crop_guidance.note: The NCERT source says arid soils can become cultivable with proper irrigation, but does not give a universal crop list. Crop choice also depends on local water availability and salinity, neither of which this image measures.
crop_guidance.source_title: NCERT, Contemporary India-II, Chapter 1: Resources and Development — Arid Soils

Black Soil.description: A visual class often associated with dark, clay-rich soils; the image does not confirm clay content or shrink-swell behavior.
characteristics: Some black soils retain substantial water and may crack when dry.
Workability and drainage depend on the actual texture and field condition.
advantages: Water storage can benefit crops when soil structure and drainage are suitable.
limitations: Wet soil may drain or dry slowly; cracking and difficult tillage can occur.
improvements: Avoid working saturated soil and check field drainage.
Use soil-test results and local guidance before nutrient or pH amendments.

crop_guidance.note: NCERT identifies black soil as suitable for cotton. The photo label does not confirm soil depth, texture, drainage, or local climate; verify those before planting.
crop_guidance.source_title: NCERT, Contemporary India-II, Chapter 1: Resources and Development — Black Soil

Laterite Soil.description: A broad weathered-soil label. Acidity, nutrient status, depth, and texture are not determined from a photograph.
characteristics: Highly weathered profiles can vary widely in nutrient retention and drainage.
A red or yellow appearance is not a measurement of soil chemistry.
advantages: Crop performance depends on local depth, water supply, and verified soil properties.
limitations: Leaching, acidity, shallow depth, or low nutrient reserves may occur at some sites.
improvements: Test pH and available nutrients before selecting amendments.
Keep soil covered and manage runoff on sloping land.

crop_guidance.note: NCERT describes tea and coffee as options with appropriate soil conservation, and cashew for red laterite soils in parts of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, and Kerala. Check local suitability; the image label does not confirm these conditions.
crop_guidance.source_title: NCERT, Contemporary India-II, Chapter 1: Resources and Development — Laterite Soil

Mountain Soil.description: A broad landscape label for mountain-region soils; properties vary with parent material, slope, and elevation.
characteristics: Soil depth, stoniness, drainage, and temperature can change over short distances.
A photograph cannot measure slope stability or erosion risk.
advantages: Suitability depends on the specific site and locally adapted crops.
limitations: Shallow soils, steep slopes, and erosion may constrain cultivation.
improvements: Use contour-aligned cover and avoid exposing steep soil to runoff.
Check soil depth, drainage, and local land-use guidance.

crop_guidance.note: Mountain soils vary with elevation, slope, and valley position. The cited NCERT source does not give one crop list for this broad label; use local altitude- and season-specific agricultural guidance.
crop_guidance.source_title: NCERT, Contemporary India-II, Chapter 1: Resources and Development — Forest Soils

Red Soil.description: A broad visual class commonly associated with iron-oxide coloration; texture and fertility vary.
characteristics: Color alone cannot establish nutrient supply, organic matter, or water retention.
Texture and drainage should be checked in the field or with a soil test.
advantages: Crop choice can be matched to measured soil properties and local rainfall.
limitations: Some sites have low organic matter or limited water retention, but this is not universal.
improvements: Use soil-test results to guide nutrients and pH management.
Retain crop residue and use cover to reduce erosion and moisture loss.

crop_guidance.note: The cited NCERT source describes red soils but does not provide a universal crop list. Crop choice needs local rainfall, texture, irrigation, and season information; soil colour alone is not enough.
crop_guidance.source_title: NCERT, Contemporary India-II, Chapter 1: Resources and Development — Red and Yellow Soils

Yellow Soil.description: A broad visual class associated with yellowish coloration. Drainage, texture, and nutrient status cannot be inferred reliably from color alone.
characteristics: Color may be affected by minerals, moisture, and drainage conditions.
The model label does not determine soil fertility or crop suitability.
advantages: Potential uses depend on measured properties and local climate.
limitations: A photograph cannot distinguish nutrient deficiency, waterlogging, or other causes of color.
improvements: Confirm texture, pH, and nutrients with a representative soil test.
Maintain ground cover and manage drainage based on field observations.

crop_guidance.note: NCERT discusses yellow soil together with red soil and gives no separate universal crop list. This visual class alone is insufficient to identify suitable crops; check local soil and climate guidance.
crop_guidance.source_title: NCERT, Contemporary India-II, Chapter 1: Resources and Development — Red and Yellow Soils
